exact_quotes: Abstract, p. 999: 'Drawing from 120 interviews with employers as well as participant observation of a hiring committee, I argue that hiring is more than just a process of skills sorting; it is also a process of cultural matching between candidates, evaluators, and firms.'

Abstract, p. 999: 'Employers sought candidates who were not only competent but also culturally similar to themselves in terms of leisure pursuits, experiences, and self-presentation styles. Concerns about shared culture were highly salient to employers and often outweighed concerns about absolute productivity.'
p. 1000 (definition): 'cultural similarities, defined here as shared tastes, experiences, leisure pursuits, and self-presentation styles (Bourdieu 1984)'
p. 1006, law firm partner Omar: 'In our new associates, we are first and foremost looking for cultural compatibility. Someone who . . . will fit in.'

p. 1007: 'Evaluators described fit as being one of the three most important criteria they used to assess candidates in job interviews; more than half reported it was the most important criterion at the job interview stage, rating fit over analytical thinking and communication.'
p. 1007, consultant Priya: 'I don't think [fit] should be [a consideration] at all, it seems to me a very [shakes her head] American thing. But it's what [firms] want, so it's what you do.'

p. 1007: 'the notion of fit evaluators in this study used differs from this conception because here it typically referred to individuals' play styles (how applicants preferred to conduct themselves outside the office) rather than their work styles.' (Original uses dashes around the parenthetical.)
p. 1007, law firm partner Vivian: 'When I hire an associate, what I want to know is, is this person someone I could be sitting across the table from at 2 a.m. when trying to get a brief done?'

p. 1008: evaluators 'commonly described their work as "not rocket science" and cited the extensive training given to new hires as minimizing the importance of prior technical knowledge for job success.'

p. 1008, banker Nicholae: 'A lot of this job is attitude, not aptitude . . . fit is really important. . . . So you can be the smartest guy ever, but I don't care. I need to be comfortable working everyday with you, then getting stuck in an airport with you, and then going for a beer after. You need chemistry. Not only that the person is smart, but that you like him.'
p. 1008, banking director Mark: 'We try to hedge our bets. Through the recruiting process, we want to find those people . . . who will fit in so that once they get here, they will not leave.'
p. 1009: 'In essence, firms sought surface-level (i.e., demographic) diversity in applicant pools but deep-level (i.e., cultural) homogeneity in new hires.'

p. 1009, Holt manager Hans arguing against a second-round invite: 'He did well on the case and was very articulate. He's a very interesting guy with a good story. But I think he's too intellectual for [FIRM]. You know, he is very into 18th-century literature and avant-garde film. . . . I don't think he'd be a good fit.' Rivera: 'The candidate was not invited back.'
p. 1010: 'roughly four-fifths of evaluators used a heuristic known as the "airplane test," which HR often endorsed.'

p. 1010, banking director Max: 'Would I want to be stuck in an airport in Minneapolis in a snowstorm with them? . . . And you also have to have some basic criteria, skills and smarts or whatever, but you know, but if they meet that test, it's most important for me.'
p. 1010, attorney Carlos: 'You . . . use yourself to measure [fit] because that's all you have to go on.'

p. 1011: 'the emphasis on fit did not increase with the client- or team-facing demands of the job; fit was least important in consulting, where work is most interpersonally focused, and it was most important in law, which has the least interpersonal demands during the first years on the job.'

p. 1011: 'the importance of fit decreased with the inclusion of technical questions in interviews. ... case interviews reduced but did not eliminate the use of cultural fit in hiring; 40 percent of consultants still ranked fit first.'
p. 1011, consultant Naveen: 'Even if someone's a perfect fit, if they absolutely bombed the case, they're out.'
p. 1012: 'Once candidates demonstrated a baseline of competence, perceptions of fit rather than absolute case performance routinely drove assessments.'
p. 1012, manager Perry: 'quite frankly, his case performance wasn't the best. But because his personality and presence were so strong, I forwarded him on [to second-round interviews].'

p. 1012: assessors 'purposefully used their own experiences as models of merit ... Essentially, they constructed merit in a manner that validated their own strengths and experiences and perceived similar candidates as better applicants.'
p. 1014, banking recruiting head Stephanie: 'You are basically hiring yourself. This is not an objective process.'
p. 1014, banker Sandeep on a mock resume: 'She plays squash. Anyone who plays squash I love.' (he 'immediately ranked her first')

p. 1015, banker Max: 'You know, if I'm really hitting it off with them, I won't give them the numbers because I don't want to see them flounder. I want to be able to go back and say, "Things went well" and pass them on.'
p. 1015: 'candidates needed to have a champion (an evaluator who would fight for them in deliberations) to receive a job offer.' (Original uses dashes around the parenthetical.)

p. 1018: 'interviewers often privileged their personal feelings of comfort, validation, and excitement over identifying candidates with superior cognitive or technical skills. In many respects, they hired in a manner more closely resembling the choice of friends or romantic partners than how sociologists typically portray employers selecting new workers.'
p. 1018: 'Whether selecting on cultural similarities produces better or worse organizational performance is outside the scope of this article.'
p. 1019: 'they might be motivated to hire the most enjoyable over the most competent candidates; that is, they may hire for themselves rather than for the organization.'
date_and_recency: Published December 2012 (ASR 77(6)). Interviews conducted 2006-2008; participant observation over nine months in 2006 and 2007. Pre-dates AI-assisted coding entirely; refers to entry-level hiring at US elite banks, law firms and consulting firms in the mid-2000s.
key_claims: Hiring in elite professional service firms is not only skills sorting but 'cultural matching' between candidates, evaluators and firms.
Cultural fit was a formal, firm-mandated evaluative criterion, not just personal taste; firms required evaluators to rate fit alongside technical and communication skills.

'Fit' as used meant similarity in play styles (leisure pursuits, extracurriculars such as lacrosse, squash, marathons), background experiences and self-presentation, not work styles or values; evaluators separated it from client-facing 'polish'.

Evaluators justified fit by long hours (wanting colleagues as 'playmates' or friends) and by retention; they described the work as 'not rocket science' and believed training made prior technical knowledge less important.

Fit was measured two ways: similarity to the firm's perceived personality (more common in resume screens) and similarity to the evaluator's own self (more common in interviews), e.g. the 'airplane test' and icebreaker chat seeking shared experiences.

Three processes link similarity to outcomes: organizational (fit as formal criterion), cognitive ('looking-glass merit', evaluators define merit in their own image), and affective (shared interests create a 'spark' that makes evaluators champion a candidate in deliberations).
Fit mattered more in less structured interviews: most in law (pure conversation), least in consulting (case interviews), and it did not track the interpersonal demands of the job.

Structured technical case questions reduced but did not remove fit; once a baseline of competence was met, fit rather than absolute case performance routinely drove decisions, and some interviewers lowered the technical bar for candidates they liked.

Consequences: firms seek demographic diversity but cultural homogeneity; valued signals are tied to white upper-middle-class, parent-funded leisure, creating inequality by parental class and some gendered disadvantage, even though women and minorities with the right signals were hired.
Selecting on play-style similarity may lead evaluators to 'hire for themselves rather than for the organization'; effect on organizational performance is untested.
headline_figures: 120 interviews with professionals involved in hiring, 40 per industry (investment banks, law firms, management consulting), 2006-2008 (p. 1005).

'more than half' of evaluators reported fit was the most important criterion at the job interview stage, 'rating fit over analytical thinking and communication' (p. 1007); next most common criteria were interpersonal polish/presence, then analytic skills (note 13).

Figure 2 (p. 1011), evaluators who force-ranked fit as most important interview criterion: law firms N = 30, investment banks N = 26, consulting firms N = 16, out of 40 per industry. Text confirms '40 percent of consultants still ranked fit first'. Law 75 percent and banks 65 percent are derived from N/40 and the chart axis, not stated in prose [uncertain].

Figure 1 (p. 1006): share of the 120 interviewees who spontaneously used each similarity process: organizational N = 117 (most prevalent, stated in text); the other two bars are N = 107 and N = 94, which from the chart layout appear to be affective = 107 and cognitive = 94 [uncertain: text extraction does not tie these labels to bars unambiguously].
'roughly four-fifths of evaluators' used the 'airplane test' (p. 1010).

Interviews lasted 40 to 90 minutes; first-round candidate interviews last 20 to 45 minutes with one or two employees; final round is three to six back-to-back interviews; consulting cases run 20 to 30 minutes (pp. 1004-1005).

Entry-level total compensation (Table 1, 2012 sources): law JD $175-330K; banking BA $70-150K, MBA/JD/PhD $150-350K; consulting BA $70-100K, MBA/JD/PhD $135-200K; 'double to quadruple' what peers from the same universities earn elsewhere (p. 1003).
sample_and_method: Qualitative case study. 120 semi-structured interviews (2006-2008) with hiring partners, managing directors, mid-level interviewers/resume screeners and HR managers at top-tier US investment banks, law firms and consulting firms (40 each), recruited by stratified sampling from directories plus referral chains. Interviews probed evaluative criteria (Lamont protocol), recent interviewees, and evaluations of mock resumes varied on sex, ethnicity, school prestige, GPA, prior employer and extracurriculars (not an experiment). Plus nine months of participant observation as an unpaid 'recruiting intern' in one firm ('Holt Halliday'): attended events, debriefed evaluators, sat in on hiring committee deliberations, but not in interviews themselves (IRB and firm restriction). Inductive grounded-theory coding in ATLAS.ti; code frequencies counted. Not software engineers: entry-level bankers, lawyers and consultants hired from elite campuses.
what_is_measured: Not a validation study of any format. It documents what evaluators actually assessed under the label 'fit' (team fit/culture fit): perceived similarity to the firm and to the interviewer in leisure pursuits, experiences and self-presentation, judged through unstructured conversation, the 'airplane test' and resume extracurriculars. Contrasted with analytic/technical skill (case interviews, finance probes) and client 'polish'.
scope_and_status: Not applicable as an interview format rollout. Describes standard practice across elite US banks, law firms and consulting firms for entry-level on-campus recruitment; observation limited to one firm.
validity_evidence: None. No criterion-validity data for fit or any interview format. Rivera states organizational performance effects are 'outside the scope of this article'. She notes (citing Rivera 2009) that at Holt resume characteristics predicted neither interview evaluations nor hiring decisions, and cites Reskin and McBrier (2000) that structured formats reduce subjectivity; the paper itself shows structured case questions reduced reliance on fit but offers no predictive-validity numbers.
relevance_to_angle: Complicates the 'communication and team fit' strand most directly: unstructured fit assessment in practice drifted into similarity-to-the-interviewer on play styles (sports, hobbies, shared schools), with evaluators lowering the technical bar for people they clicked with. If Lee argues for moving interviews away from convergent coding toward conversation and team fit, this is the strongest warning that fit, left unstructured, becomes 'hiring yourself'. It also partly supports keeping some structured, job-relevant test (the case interview reduced fit's weight: 40 percent of consultants vs. far more in law). Useful for framing team fit as defined work-style criteria (how someone collaborates, communicates and reasons) rather than likeability; Rivera herself suggests comparing 'similarity in work styles, which can be beneficial ... versus play styles'.
limitations_stated: Stated scope conditions (p. 1016-1017): 'My intent was not to develop a universal theory of hiring'; evaluators do not choose their interviewees; they interview for positions below them; 'given that cultural fit was strongest in firms that employed open-ended interviews, selection on cultural similarity should be tampered in highly standardized or technical hiring evaluations'; results may show more sex or race bias where culture and demography are more tightly coupled. Elite focus 'constrains generalizability' and 'may magnify the relative importance of cultural similarities' (p. 1003). Observed only one firm and could not sit in on interviews (p. 1005). Author notes her identity 'may have primed respondents to emphasize high-status cultural practices (which they did) and favor diversity (which they did not)' (p. 1005). Performance effects untested (p. 1018).
counter_evidence: Within the paper: case interviews reduced fit's weight, and Naveen's 'if they absolutely bombed the case, they're out' shows a technical floor still bit. Women and minorities were hired at higher rates than white men at Holt, so cultural matching here was not simply race or sex homophily. Rivera concedes cultural similarity can facilitate trust and communication in team-heavy work and that work-style fit can be beneficial (Chatman 1991). Broader literature (not opened here) on person-organization fit reports links to satisfaction and retention; Rivera cites Chatman (1991) for 'employee satisfaction, performance, and retention' [uncertain: Chatman not opened]. Evidence is interview self-report and one firm's deliberations, not hiring outcome data across firms, and is from a non-software, elite-campus context in 2006-2008.
